lessonTitle: Phase I and Phase II Metabolism: Cytochrome P450, Conjugation, First-Pass Effect and Prodrugs

blocks.text: To slow a racing heart in an emergency, a doctor might give propranolol by vein in a dose of about 1 mg. To control blood pressure with the same drug, a patient swallows a tablet of 40 mg or more. Forty times the dose for a similar effect: the difference is the liver, which removes much of an oral dose before it reaches the rest of the body.

blocks.markdown: **Drug metabolism** converts lipid-soluble drugs into more water-soluble compounds that can be excreted in urine or bile. It occurs mainly in the liver, with contributions from the gut wall, kidney and lung. Metabolism is divided into **phase I** (functionalisation) and **phase II** (conjugation). Metabolites are usually less active, but not always.

blocks.title: Phase I and phase II reactions
blocks.text: Phase I reactions introduce or expose a functional group (such as -OH, -NH2 or -COOH) by oxidation, reduction or hydrolysis; the most important enzymes are the cytochrome P450 (CYP) family. Phase II reactions conjugate the drug or its phase I metabolite with a polar endogenous molecule such as glucuronic acid, sulfate, glutathione or an acetyl group, greatly increasing water solubility.

blocks.caption: Phase I compared with phase II metabolism.
rows: Conjugation (glucuronidation, sulfation, acetylation, glutathione conjugation, methylation)
Cytochrome P450 (CYP3A4, CYP2D6, CYP2C9, CYP2C19), esterases
Small increase in polarity; metabolite may be active, inactive or toxic
Large increase in polarity; metabolite usually inactive and readily excreted
Diazepam demethylated to nordiazepam; paracetamol oxidised to NAPQI (minor pathway)
Paracetamol glucuronidation and sulfation (major pathways); morphine glucuronidation
Often induced or inhibited by other drugs; genetic polymorphism (CYP2D6, CYP2C19)

blocks.title: Following a drug through both phases
blocks.prompt: Paracetamol at therapeutic doses is eliminated mainly by phase II conjugation, with a small fraction oxidised by CYP enzymes. Describe the fate of paracetamol and explain why a phase I product is of concern.

steps.text: Most paracetamol (the large majority) is conjugated directly by UGT enzymes to paracetamol glucuronide and by sulfotransferases to paracetamol sulfate. These phase II products are inactive and water soluble, so they are excreted in urine.
A small fraction is oxidised by CYP enzymes (phase I) to the reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI).
At normal doses NAPQI is rapidly conjugated with glutathione (a phase II reaction) and excreted harmlessly.

In overdose the phase II pathways saturate, more NAPQI forms and glutathione is depleted, so NAPQI binds to hepatocytes and causes liver necrosis. A phase I product can therefore be more toxic than the parent drug.

blocks.answer: Most is conjugated and excreted safely; a small phase I product (NAPQI) is detoxified by glutathione but causes liver injury in overdose.

blocks.markdown: **First-pass effect.** A drug absorbed from the gut passes via the portal vein through the liver before reaching the systemic circulation. If the liver (and gut wall) metabolise a large fraction on this first passage, oral bioavailability is reduced. Bioavailability is the product of the fraction absorbed from the gut (fa), the fraction escaping gut wall metabolism (fg) and the fraction escaping hepatic metabolism (fh), where fh = 1 minus the hepatic extraction ratio E.

blocks.latex: F = f_a \times f_g \times f_h, \qquad f_h = 1 - E
blocks.caption: F = oral bioavailability; fa = fraction absorbed; fg = fraction escaping gut wall metabolism; fh = fraction escaping hepatic extraction; E = hepatic extraction ratio (0 to 1).

blocks.title: Calculating oral bioavailability with first-pass loss
blocks.prompt: A drug has fa = 0.9, fg = 0.8 and hepatic extraction ratio E = 0.5. Calculate F, and the amount reaching the circulation after a 100 mg oral dose. (Teaching example.)

steps.text: Calculate fh from the extraction ratio.
Amount reaching the systemic circulation = 100 mg x 0.36 = 36 mg.
The rest (64 mg) is lost by incomplete absorption, gut wall metabolism or hepatic first-pass metabolism. A drug with E near 1 would have very low oral bioavailability.

blocks.answer: F = 0.36, so 36 mg of a 100 mg oral dose reaches the circulation

items: High first-pass drugs include propranolol, glyceryl trinitrate, lidocaine and morphine; oral doses are much larger than IV doses.
Routes that avoid first pass: intravenous, sublingual, transdermal, inhaled, subcutaneous, intramuscular; the lower rectum partly avoids it.
Liver disease or portosystemic shunting reduces first-pass loss, so oral bioavailability and effect may rise unexpectedly.
Enzyme inducers and inhibitors alter first-pass metabolism and therefore oral bioavailability.

blocks.title: Prodrug
blocks.text: A prodrug is an inactive or weakly active compound that is converted in the body, by metabolism, into the active drug. Examples are enalapril (hydrolysed by esterases to enalaprilat) and valaciclovir (converted to aciclovir). Prodrugs may improve absorption, bioavailability or targeting.

blocks.markdown: **Why prodrugs?** Enalaprilat, the active ACE inhibitor, is poorly absorbed orally because it is highly polar. Enalapril is an ethyl ester that is better absorbed and is then hydrolysed in the liver to enalaprilat. Valaciclovir is the valine ester of aciclovir and gives considerably higher oral bioavailability of aciclovir through intestinal transporters. Because activation depends on enzymes, impaired liver function or genetic variants may reduce the effect of a prodrug.

blocks.title: Metabolites are not always inactive
blocks.text: Some metabolites are active (morphine-6-glucuronide, nordiazepam) and may accumulate in renal failure, prolonging effects. Metabolism does not always mean detoxification.

points: Phase I reactions (mainly CYP oxidation) expose a functional group; phase II reactions conjugate with a polar molecule to make the drug water soluble and usually inactive.
First-pass metabolism by gut wall and liver reduces oral bioavailability (F = fa x fg x fh); routes that bypass the portal circulation avoid it.
A prodrug is activated by metabolism, as with enalapril converted to enalaprilat, and may offer better absorption.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes phase I drug metabolism?

options.text: It introduces or exposes a functional group, mainly by cytochrome P450 oxidation
It attaches glucuronic acid to a functional group
It always produces an inactive metabolite
It occurs only in the kidney

questions.correctOptionText: It introduces or exposes a functional group, mainly by cytochrome P450 oxidation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: phase I functionalisation includes oxidation, reduction and hydrolysis.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: phase I metabolites may be active or toxic.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: the liver is the main site.

questions.explanation: Phase I reactions add or reveal a reactive group on the drug, mainly through CYP-mediated oxidation. This prepares the molecule for phase II conjugation, but the product can be active or toxic.

questions.stem: Which description fits a phase II reaction?

options.text: Glucuronidation of morphine by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase, increasing water solubility
Hydroxylation of a drug by CYP3A4
Hydrolysis of an ester by plasma esterase
Reduction of a nitro group by gut bacteria

questions.correctOptionText: Glucuronidation of morphine by UDP-glucuronosyltransferase, increasing water solubility

distractorRationale.a: Correct: conjugation with glucuronic acid is a classical phase II reaction.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: CYP hydroxylation is phase I.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: reduction is a phase I type reaction.

questions.explanation: Phase II reactions attach a large polar group such as glucuronic acid to the drug, hugely increasing solubility and aiding excretion. Oxidation, reduction and hydrolysis are phase I.

questions.stem: A newborn infant given a standard adult-scaled dose of chloramphenicol becomes grey, hypotensive and collapses. Which mechanism best explains the toxicity?

options.text: Immature glucuronidation (phase II) in neonates, so the drug accumulates

questions.correctOptionText: Immature glucuronidation (phase II) in neonates, so the drug accumulates

distractorRationale.a: Correct: neonates have low UGT activity, so chloramphenicol is poorly conjugated and accumulates.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: induction would lower, not raise, levels.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: reduced, not increased, metabolism explains the accumulation.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: chloramphenicol is not a prodrug.

questions.explanation: Glucuronidation is immature in the newborn, so drugs that rely on it, such as chloramphenicol, are cleared slowly. Toxic levels produce cardiovascular collapse, known as grey baby syndrome.

questions.stem: A drug is completely absorbed from the gut and not metabolised in the gut wall. It has a hepatic extraction ratio of 0.6. How many milligrams of a 200 mg oral dose reach the systemic circulation? (Teaching example.)
questions.explanation: fh = 1 - E = 0.4 and fa = fg = 1, so F = 0.4. The amount reaching the circulation is 200 x 0.4 = 80 mg; the other 120 mg is removed in first-pass hepatic metabolism.

questions.stem: A drug has fa = 0.85, fg = 1.0 and a hepatic extraction ratio of 0.6. Calculate the oral bioavailability F as a fraction.
questions.explanation: fh = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4. F = fa x fg x fh = 0.85 x 1.0 x 0.4 = 0.34, so about a third of the oral dose reaches the systemic circulation.

questions.stem: A patient is stable on an intravenous dose of 10 mg of a drug. The drug's oral bioavailability is 0.3. Assuming otherwise equal exposure is needed, calculate the equivalent oral dose in milligrams. (Teaching example.)
questions.explanation: Oral dose = IV dose / F = 10 / 0.3 = 33.3 mg. The larger oral dose compensates for first-pass loss and is why oral doses of high-extraction drugs are much greater than IV doses.

questions.stem: Enalapril is given to a patient with hypertension and is converted to enalaprilat in the liver. How is enalapril best described?

options.text: An active drug inactivated by hydrolysis
A drug that is activated by glucuronidation

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the ester is hydrolysed to the active enalaprilat.
distractorRationale.b: Incorrect: hydrolysis activates rather than inactivates enalapril.
distractorRationale.c: Incorrect: metabolism is required for activity.
distractorRationale.d: Incorrect: activation is by ester hydrolysis, not glucuronidation.

questions.explanation: Enalapril is an inactive ester that is hydrolysed to enalaprilat, the active ACE inhibitor. The ester form is better absorbed orally than the polar active compound.

questions.stem: Describe the first-pass effect and its impact on oral bioavailability, naming two routes that avoid it.
markingGuide: Drug absorbed from the gut enters the portal vein and passes through the liver before reaching the systemic circulation
Gut wall and hepatic enzymes metabolise a fraction, reducing the amount reaching the circulation
Oral bioavailability F = fa x fg x fh, where fh = 1 minus hepatic extraction ratio
High extraction drugs (propranolol, glyceryl trinitrate, lidocaine) need much larger oral than IV doses
Routes avoiding first pass: sublingual, intravenous, transdermal, inhaled, intramuscular or subcutaneous; lower rectum partly
questions.explanation: First-pass metabolism removes drug before it reaches the systemic circulation, lowering oral bioavailability. Routes that deliver drug directly to systemic veins bypass this loss.

questions.stem: Explain what is meant by a prodrug, using valaciclovir or enalapril as an example, and state one advantage and one disadvantage of prodrugs.
markingGuide: Prodrug: inactive or weakly active compound converted by metabolism into the active drug
Example: enalapril is hydrolysed by esterases to enalaprilat, or valaciclovir to aciclovir
Advantage: improved absorption or bioavailability (the active compound is too polar to be absorbed well)
Disadvantage: depends on enzyme activation, so effect may vary with liver function or genetic variants, or with interacting drugs
Link to metabolism: activation is typically a phase I reaction such as hydrolysis
questions.explanation: Prodrug design uses the body's own enzymes to release the active molecule at or after absorption. The cost is dependence on that conversion, which can differ between patients.

questions.stem: True or false: phase II conjugation always converts a drug into a pharmacologically inactive metabolite.
questions.explanation: Most conjugates are inactive, but some retain activity; for example morphine-6-glucuronide is an active analgesic metabolite and can accumulate in renal failure. Metabolism therefore does not always equal inactivation.
